packs.name: Atlas
packs.tagline: Six hundred instruments, in sixty-six megabytes.
packs.subtitle: The whole instrument world, in one download.
packs.description: Atlas is the entire General MIDI world in a single file, and then some. Every one of the 128 standard instruments is here, from concert grand to sitar to timpani, and behind almost all of them sit further characters: a brighter piano, a darker string section, a second and third voice for the same instrument across forty-six variation banks. That comes to 601 playable instruments in sixty-six megabytes, about a tenth of a megabyte each. Every preset was loaded and rendered before release, and the ten that came back silent were dropped rather than shipped.

highlights.title: Everything, not a selection
highlights.detail: All 128 General MIDI instruments, plus 473 further variations. Most banks give you one piano. This gives you a shelf of them.

highlights.title: A tenth of a megabyte per instrument
highlights.detail: Sixty-six megabytes covers ground that usually costs several gigabytes.

highlights.title: Recorded at full rate
highlights.detail: Of its 1,021 samples, 92 percent are 44.1 kHz and the rest are 48 kHz. Nothing was downsampled to save room.

highlights.title: Public domain, genuinely
highlights.detail: Released under CC0 and built from open sample libraries that are themselves public domain.

packs.name: Orchestra & World
packs.tagline: Three hundred recorded instruments, from the concert hall outward.
packs.subtitle: The orchestra, the choir, and the world beyond them.
packs.description: Orchestra & World is the large, serious library: strings and brass and woodwinds recorded as sections and as soloists, a choir that holds as long as you hold your hands apart, pipe organs, and a long tail of instruments from outside the western orchestra. It is the biggest download Sonari offers and the one with the most range inside it. Every preset was rendered before release and the four that came back silent were dropped.

highlights.title: The orchestra, section by section
highlights.detail: Strings, brass and woodwinds as full sections and as individual players, so you can score rather than sketch.

highlights.title: A choir that breathes with you
highlights.detail: Held vocal sections on ah and ooh, which under hand control become the most expressive thing in the app.

highlights.title: Well past the concert hall
highlights.detail: Sitar, koto, shamisen, kalimba, bagpipes and more, recorded rather than modelled.

packs.name: Vintage FM
packs.tagline: The sound of a 1990s sound card, done properly.
packs.subtitle: 129 FM instruments with the grain left in.
packs.description: Vintage FM is the OPL-3 chip: the synthesis that scored a decade of games and demos, before sampling took over. It is not an imitation of acoustic instruments and never was. Its brass is glassy, its basses bite, and its bells have a metallic edge no recording gives you. All 129 of its instruments were rendered before release and all 129 sounded, with none dropped.

highlights.title: A sound with a decade attached
highlights.detail: Frequency modulation, not recordings. Instantly placeable and impossible to reach with a sample library.

highlights.title: All 129 verified
highlights.detail: Every preset was loaded and rendered before release. None were dropped, because none needed dropping.

highlights.title: A complete layout
highlights.detail: The whole General MIDI map in FM, so any part written for it plays through without gaps.

packs.name: Session Band
packs.tagline: The band in the room, one hundred and eighty-eight ways.
packs.subtitle: Warm, played, and built for songs.
packs.description: Session Band is the rhythm section and everything around it: drums that sit back, basses with weight, guitars that were played rather than programmed, and keys that suit a song instead of a score. It is the warmest of Sonari's banks and the one to reach for when you are writing rather than orchestrating. All 189 presets were rendered before release and the one that came back silent was dropped.

highlights.title: Played, not programmed
highlights.detail: Guitars, basses and drums recorded by musicians, with the hand noise and the room left in.

highlights.title: MIT licensed
highlights.detail: Free for any use including commercial, and one of the very few banks whose provenance has been reviewed by Debian for inclusion in its main archive.

highlights.title: Twenty-five years of refinement
highlights.detail: In continuous use and maintenance since 2000, which is why it still sounds right under almost anything.

packs.name: Concert Grand Piano
packs.tagline: One piano, sampled until it stopped being a sample.
packs.description: Most sampled pianos give you three or four levels of loudness and cross-fade between them, which is why they go glassy when you lean in. This one was captured at sixteen, note by note, so the distance between a whisper and a shout is a continuum rather than four steps. In the air that matters more than it does at a keyboard: your hand's height is a smooth control, and this is the one instrument in the library with enough recorded detail to answer it smoothly back.
content: The most detailed instrument Sonari offers
packs.license: Salamander Grand Piano by Alexander Holm, CC-BY 3.0.
packs.subtitle: Sixteen dynamic layers, and a hand that can reach all of them.

highlights.title: Sixteen layers, not four
highlights.detail: Loudness is recorded, not faked with a filter, so leaning in changes the tone and not just the volume.

highlights.title: One instrument, done completely
highlights.detail: Every note captured separately. Nothing here is a neighbouring key played faster or slower.

highlights.title: Honest about its size
highlights.detail: It is the largest download on the shelf by a wide margin, and it is the only one that needs to be.

packs.name: Spanish Guitar
packs.tagline: Nylon strings, close enough to hear the nails.
packs.description: A real classical guitar, miked close enough that you get the fingertip on the string before the note arrives. That attack is what makes a plucked instrument legible in the air: a hand crossing a note boundary produces a real pluck rather than a fade, so playing this with gestures sounds like playing rather than like sweeping a synthesiser. It suits slow lines and it suits being hit hard.
content: Close-recorded, with the fingers left in
packs.subtitle: A classical guitar recorded at conversation distance.

highlights.title: The fingers are in the recording
highlights.detail: String noise and nail attack were kept, which is what separates a recorded guitar from a synthesised one.

highlights.title: Made for plucking in the air
highlights.detail: A crisp attack means every note lands, and every note boundary a hand crosses is audible as a new pluck.

packs.name: Hang Drum
packs.tagline: Struck air, and a very long ring.
packs.description: The handpan is the one acoustic instrument that seems to have been designed for playing without touching anything. Its notes bloom rather than start, it holds for seconds, and it is tuned so that almost nothing you play is wrong. Slow hands sound deliberate on it and fast hands sound like rain. If you are showing somebody what playing in the air is, do it on this.
content: A real handpan in D minor
packs.subtitle: The most gesture-native instrument in the library.

highlights.title: Nothing you play is wrong
highlights.detail: Tuned so its notes agree with each other, which makes it forgiving in a way no keyboard instrument is.

highlights.title: Notes that bloom
highlights.detail: A soft attack and a long ring, so slow hand movement reads as musical rather than as hesitation.

packs.name: Glass
packs.tagline: Played glass: pure, airy, and very still.
packs.description: Glass instruments are almost pure tone with almost no attack, which makes them the opposite of the guitar: nothing here is percussive, and everything drifts. That turns a hand's position into something closer to a fader than a key, and it is the reason this pack is worth having even though it holds one instrument. Play it slowly, high up, with plenty of space, and it does not sound like a sample library at all.
packs.subtitle: The quietest thing on the shelf, and the most spatial.

highlights.title: Tone without a strike
highlights.detail: Hardly any attack, so a hand moving through it glides rather than triggers.

highlights.title: Room to sit in
highlights.detail: Spatial and quiet, which makes it the natural bed under anything else you are playing.

packs.name: Kalimba
packs.tagline: Thumb-plucked metal, with the wood behind it.
packs.description: A real kalimba: metal tines over a wooden box, so every note has a bright ping and a low woody knock underneath it. It is small in every sense, which is the point. Ten megabytes, one instrument, and a sound so recognisable that a few notes of it establish a whole piece. Like the handpan it is tuned to be forgiving, so it rewards playing quickly without planning.
content: Metal tines over a wooden body
packs.subtitle: Small, bright, and impossible to play badly.

highlights.title: Bright on top, wooden underneath
highlights.detail: Two sounds in every note: the tine's ping and the body's knock. Both were recorded.

highlights.title: Ten megabytes
highlights.detail: The smallest download on the shelf, and complete.

packs.name: Living Notes
packs.tagline: Visuals that move with your melody.
packs.description: Hundreds of musical visuals built around notes themselves: constellations that chart your chords, auroras that breathe with your phrasing, geometry that turns scales into structure. Every visual listens to velocity, bend, and pressure, so what you see is always what you played.

packs.name: Natural Forces
packs.tagline: Water, gravity, fire and light that answer your hands.
packs.description: The physics collection: fluids that ripple where notes land, marble veined by your harmony, particle storms kicked by every attack, and lattices that bend under tension. Play gently and the world settles; play hard and it erupts.

packs.name: Painted Worlds
packs.tagline: Art history as a living canvas.
packs.description: From Starry Night swirls to hard-edge minimalism: forty-eight painting styles reimagined as instruments. Brushwork follows your melody, palettes shift with your key, and every era answers your dynamics in its own voice.
